As of 330 PM EST Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Scattered showers are possible later this 
afternoon into tonight along and behind a strong cold front.

Latest surface analysis depicted a cold front just to the NW of
the local area with plentiful clearing ahead of the front and 
temps as of 1 PM in the low-mid 70s across the NW half of the 
area and upper 60s to lower 70s across the SE half. Highs this 
afternoon are expected to be a degree or two higher. The strong 
cold front pushes across the area later this afternoon into 
tonight with winds becoming N 10-15 mph with gusts up to 20-25 
mph (gusts up to 30 mph are possible along the coast). CAMs 
continue to show the potential for scattered showers developing 
along and behind the front (largely anafrontal in nature). As 
such, have PoPs increasing to 30-45% for most of the area 
tonight with a brief period of 50-60% PoPs across far SE VA/NE 
NC around midnight. Showers should remain light with rainfall 
totals generally below 0.1-0.2". Showers move offshore by around
sunrise Tue morning. Given the cloud cover and breezy winds 
tonight, think the NBM is too cool with lows. As such have lows 
in the upper 30s NW to upper 40s to around 50F SE. 

Much cooler temperatures are expected on Tue with highs in the 
50s. The biggest change for the forecast for Tue is that 12z 
CAMs now show the potential for widespread cloud cover across 
most of the area during the afternoon (due to cirrus). As such, 
increased cloud cover and now have mostly cloudy skies Tue 
afternoon along and east of I-95. Clouds are expected to move 
offshore by Tue night with clear skies allowing for lows in the 
upper 20s NW to mid 30s SE inland and low-mid 40s across far SE 
VA/NE NC. However, will note that winds may be elevated enough 
to keep lows a bit warmer than the current NBM lows. Otherwise, 
Tue is the driest day of the week with min RH of 25-35% inland.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Confidence continues to increase regarding an 
impactful storm across the region late Wednesday into 
Thanksgiving Day with heavy rain and strong winds increasingly 
likely.

12z guidance remains in strong agreement showing strong high 
pressure (1040+mb) setting up over New England on Wednesday with
low pressure developing off the Southeast coast. This low is 
forecast to lift northward through the afternoon into the 
overnight period, setting up a strong pressure gradient over the
area. NE winds will strengthen through the day and into the 
overnight, especially at the coast. Low level moisture increases
as well with PoPs increasing across the south late Wed 
afternoon, spreading northward after sunset. There remains some 
disagreement on the complex upper level pattern with respect to 
how much phasing occurs between the northern and southern jet 
shortwaves. The GFS keeps the shortwaves separate whereas the 
EURO phases them. However, even with different upper level 
patterns, both models (and respective ensembles) have a very 
similar track of the low, with most ensemble members taking the 
low inland across NC and VA. Therefore, while there is still 
spread by the time the low gets to VA, it will be an impactful 
storm regardless of a western or eastern track across the local 
area. 

While the forecast only goes out through Thu afternoon for 
rain, NBM still has 1.5-2" of rain across the N/NW portion of 
the FA with 2- 2.5" of rain for most of the area and 2.5-3" of 
rain across SE VA/NE NC. Probabilities for >2" of QPF were 
50-80% on the EPS while the GEFS showed 50-70%. Additionally, 
the NBM probs for 3" or more of rain were 30-55% across the 
area. As such, confidence is increasing in a widespread, 
beneficial rain with the potential for locally heavy rain. Will 
note that most of the rain could fall within a 6 hour timeframe.
If the heavy rain rates do occur, localized flash flooding 
would be possible. As such, WPC has a marginal (level 1/5) risk 
for excessive rainfall across the area Wed (due to Wed night 
precipitation) and Thu. Rain tapers off from south to north Thu 
afternoon into Thu night as the low lifts north. Outside of the 
rain, E/ENE winds become windy on Thu with gusts up to 40-50 mph
possible inland and 50-60 mph possible along the coast. If 
these trends continue, a High Wind Watch may be needed along the
coast. Winds become SW Thu night behind the low Thu night into 
Fri, remaining breezy to windy with gusts up to 30-35 mph 
possible on Fri. With many folks likely to be traveling during 
the peak impacts from this system, users should closely monitor 
the forecast over the next 24-36 hours as details come into 
focus.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Widespread moderate to major coastal flooding 
is becoming increasingly likely Wednesday night into Friday, 
with the greatest threat during high tide Thanksgiving morning 
through midday.
